## 4. HISTORICAL NOTES

### Bartolomeu Sirvent
Secretary (*secretarius*) to Queen Violant de Bar (Yolande de Bar), wife of Joan I of Aragon. The *secretarius* held a key position in the queen's household, responsible for drafting and authenticating correspondence issued under the secret seal (*sigillum secretum*). Sirvent's tenure as documented in this register spans 1387–1390, a formative period of Joan I's reign following his accession in January 1387.

### Queen Violant de Bar (Yolande de Bar)
French princess (1365–1431), daughter of Robert I, Duke of Bar, and Marie of France. She married the future Joan I of Aragon in 1380. Known as a significant cultural patron and politically active queen consort. Her separate chancery, as evidenced by this register, reflects her autonomous administrative capacity within the Crown of Aragon's governmental structure.

### The Secret Seal (*Sigillum Secretum*)
Distinguished from the great seal (*sigillum maius*), the secret seal was used for more personal or confidential correspondence. Registers organized by seal type (*Curie Sigilli Secreti*) were standard in Crown of Aragon chancery practice.

### Document 1 — Letter to the Pope

Most Holy Father and Lord. Be it known that the most illustrious prince and lord, Lord John, by the grace of God King of Aragon, our dearest lord, has seen fit to send to Your Clemency: the Reverend Father in Christ García, Archbishop of Zaragoza, and his beloved Chamberlain and Counselor and Majordomo, Sir Pere d'Artés, knight, and Raimon de França, Doctor of Decrees, Vice-Chancellor—his counselors—for the purpose of declaring publicly, both on his behalf and on ours as his wife and spouse, as conceived [in our deliberations], that you have been legitimately and canonically elected as one Pontiff of the Holy Roman and Universal Church and as a well-deserving successor in the world, as they themselves and we have recently come to know, and [to explain] other matters touching upon the advantage and honor of the aforesaid Church and of our said lord, his [subjects] and our subjects.

[We ask] Your Sanctity [to grant] that, giving full faith to the aforesaid ambassadors concerning the aforementioned matters before Your Holiness, you deign graciously to admit and hear what they shall set forth in the name of the said Lord King and of ourselves.

[We also] send as recommended our beloved Galceran de Vilanova, Archdeacon of Besalú in the Diocese of Girona, chaplain and proctor of affairs of the said Lord King at the Roman Curia, [asking that you] hold him [in favor]. For these things, which shall come to us as a singular gift, [we pray that] He whom the heavens and the forty [?] of the world praise as a polished flower may preserve Your [Holiness] for long years. Given at Barcelona under our customary seal, on the sixth [or twenty-fourth?] day of February, in the year of the Lord 1387. The Queen.

## 4. HISTORICAL NOTES

### **The Western Schism Context (1378–1417)**
This document dates to February 1387, during the height of the Western Schism. The Crown of Aragon under Joan I (r. 1387–1396) supported the Avignon obedience and Pope **Clement VII** (Robert of Geneva, 1378–1394). The embassy described here likely relates to Joan I's formal declaration of obedience to Clement VII shortly after his accession following the death of Pere IV (Pere III of Catalonia) on 5 January 1387.

### **Persons Identified**

1. **Joan I of Aragon** (1350–1396): King of Aragon from January 1387. Known as "el Caçador" (the Hunter). The embassy described here is among the first diplomatic acts of his reign.

2. **Violant de Bar** (Yolande of Bar, c. 1365–1431): Queen consort, wife of Joan I, and the issuer of these letters. Daughter of Robert I, Duke of Bar, and Marie of France. A powerful figure in her own right, she maintained her own chancery under the secretario Bartolomeu Sirvent.

3. **García Fernández de Heredia** (d. 1411): Archbishop of Zaragoza (1383–1411). A major figure in Aragonese ecclesiastical politics, he led several diplomatic missions and later played a role in the Council of Constance.

4. **Pere d'Artés**: Knight, chamberlain (camarlenc), and majordomo to Joan I. Member of an important Valencian noble family.

5. **Ramon de França**: Doctor of Decrees, Vice-Chancellor. A trained canonist serving in the royal administration.

6. **Galceran de Vilanova**: Archdeacon of Besalú (Bisulduni), Diocese of Girona. Royal proctor at the papal curia—a key diplomatic liaison position.

7. **Bartolomeu Sirvent**: Secretary to Queen Violant, keeper of her secret seal, and registrar of this series. His name appears in the register's title folio.

### **Embassy Purpose**
The embassy's purpose was to:
1. Formally recognize Clement VII as legitimate pope (declaring "unum pontificem... legittime et canonice... electum")
2. Present the Crown's position on Church unity
3. Recommend Galceran de Vilanova as the Crown's permanent representative at Avignon

## 3. ENGLISH TRANSLATION

### Document 1:

**The Queen**

Concerning the matter of the redemption to be made of the fief of Alboyda, and the matter of certain criminals who are at present in this Kingdom of Valencia: the Lord King, our very dear husband, and we send there our faithful [servant] en Julià Garrig, sub-treasurer of the said Lord [King], [who] is more informed and more perfectly informed. Wherefore we pray and command that to the words which the said sub-treasurer shall say to you on behalf of the said Lord [King] and on our behalf concerning the said matters pertaining [to us], you give faith and grace, fully and properly, with such good compliance and profession of great companionship, and [that you] do for us, for the Lord King and for us, pleasure. And because that which he and we shall greatly thank you [for], be assured that it is a matter that we hold greatly at heart. Given at Barcelona under our ring seal, on the 20th day of March of the year 1388. Secretary.

**Violant, by the grace of God Queen of Aragon, etc. To the adelantados and to the entire aljama of our Jews of the City of Teruel, whom [God] guard.**

Our faithful [servant] Johan Ramírez de Poma will tell you [the details], who by our command goes to you, and [he will] explain at length for what just reasons [this is needed], and we command you that in all that he tells you concerning this matter on our behalf you give faith and credence, just as if we personally were telling it to you.

Given in Barcelona, [at/from?] the [point?], on the 27th day of May, in the year of the Nativity of Our Lord 1388. De[s]ponte.

**Marginal note:** A similar [letter] was made and sent to the Alcalde, alamín, councillors, and the entire aljama of the Saracens [Muslims] of [Cutanda?], likewise Teruel.

### Document 2

**The Queen.**

We have learned the other day of the [medical] crisis of the lord King, and of the grave accident [illness episode] that he has had. It has followed that the illness worsened after the moon was renewed [i.e., after the new moon], [we are] seeing fever in the said lord, and [it] has continued until today, so that things have not gone well, for since he came [here?] he has not been fully recovered.

It is true that for some days the fever has come, as one [expects?], and has come on Thursday, Friday, and Saturday just past with great distress. And among the other ailments that he has had this week, he has been unable to sleep, especially for five or six days, which has vexed [him], until today when he has rested more than on the preceding days.

We inform you of this so that you may pass [the news along?] with love, and pray devoutly to our Lord for the health of the said lord.

Given in Barcelona under our privy seal on the 27th day of May, in the year [1388]. Des[ponte]. [Scribal initial].

## 4. HISTORICAL NOTES

### Persons

**Violant de Bar (Yolande of Bar)** (c. 1365–1431): Queen consort of Aragon as wife of Joan I (r. 1387–1396). Daughter of Robert I, Duke of Bar, and Marie of France. Known for her political activity during her husband's frequent illnesses. This document provides direct evidence of her role in managing both domestic taxation and diplomatic communications during Joan's incapacity.

**Joan I of Aragon** ("el Caçador," the Hunter) (1350–1396): King of Aragon from 1387. Known for his passion for hunting and music, and for chronic health problems that left him frequently incapacitated. This letter documents a serious health crisis in May 1388, involving fever, insomnia, and "great distress" (*gran congoxa*).

**Johan Ramírez de Poma**: Royal agent tasked with collecting funds from the Jewish aljama of Teruel. Typical of the *fideles nostri* (faithful servants) employed for sensitive fiscal missions.

**Bartolomeu Sirvent**: Secretary of Queen Violant's privy seal (*sigillo secreto*), named in the register's opening rubric. He authenticated both documents on this folio.

### Places

**Teruel**: City in southern Aragon with significant Jewish and Muslim populations. The parallel letters to both the Jewish aljama and the Saracen aljama demonstrate the Crown's practice of taxing both communities for extraordinary expenses.

**Cutanda (?)**: The reading "Cuy/tan[t] Turoly" in the marginal note may refer to Cutanda, a town near Teruel with a documented Muslim community, though this reading remains uncertain.

### Context

**The King's Illness**: The detailed medical report in Document 2 describes symptoms consistent with recurring malarial fever (tertian or quartan), common in the medieval Mediterranean. The reference to the illness worsening "after the moon was renewed" reflects medieval medical beliefs linking disease cycles to lunar phases. Joan I was known to suffer from frequent illness throughout his reign.

**Ambassadors in Sicily**: The Crown of Aragon maintained close diplomatic ties with Sicily (ruled by a cadet branch of the dynasty). The dispatch of health bulletins to ambassadors abroad reflects the political sensitivity of royal illness — succession crises could be triggered by rumors of a monarch's death.

- **Capitols**: Formal agreements or chapters establishing jurisdictional and financial arrangements between crown officials. The dispute here concerns whether certain places fall under the queen's jurisdiction (and thus her officials' authority) or under some other arrangement.

- The document reflects tensions over **jurisdictional boundaries** between the queen's administration and other royal officials, specifically regarding revenues (*emoluments*) and the exercise of justice in lands where jurisdiction was divided or contested.

These letters date to early in Joan I's reign (he succeeded Pere III on 5 January 1387). The mention of the king's illness and convalescence just six months into his reign is noteworthy for understanding the political climate of 1387.

## 3. ENGLISH TRANSLATION

### Document 1
**[Address]**
To my dear mother and lady, the lady Duchess of Bar.

**[Salutation in margin]**
Lady, your humble daughter, who humbly commends herself to your grace and blessing: the Queen of Aragon.

**[Body]**
Most dear brother,¹ because we receive, as we ought, supreme pleasure and very great joy in learning of your good health and condition, and consequently we remain with present and continual desire [to hear thereof], we beseech you, as affectionately as we are able, that you deign to inform us clearly, and by your letters, whenever hereafter it may please you.

And because we know that you likewise, most dear brother, are pleased to learn good news of our condition, we inform you that we and our children—the firstborn and [the infants] Jaffo[?]—are in good disposition of our persons. And that the lord King, our most dear husband and lord, is in good convalescence from a grave illness, thanks be to our Lord, may it please Him in His mercy to restore him to full health and to restore to us his [full] cognizance.

And if from these parts hither, most dear brother, any things would please you, instruct us therein, and we shall fulfill them with good heart. Most dear brother, may the Holy Trinity be your guardian always.

Given in Barcelona under our secret seal, on the 4th day of July, in the year 1387.

This letter dates from early in Joan I's reign (he succeeded his father Pere III in January 1387). The mention of the king's illness is significant for understanding the early challenges of the reign. The emphasis on maintaining family communication with the House of Bar reflects the importance of these French connections for Aragonese diplomacy.

### Persons

**Joan I of Aragon (King):** The document describes his recovery from illness in summer 1387, shortly after his accession to the throne following Pere III's death in January 1387. Joan I was known for his fragile health throughout his reign.

**The Queen**

Very dear brother. We have received two letters—one from Sir Johan d'Ixalt and another from the Governor of Aragon—which we transmit to you in their [original] form, so that you may better see clearly what they contain on your behalf. And since, according to the reports in those [letters], your presence in Aragon is properly necessary—as you will see in the said letters—we earnestly pray you that as soon as you are able, you proceed toward that region as commanded.

And while you are there, you shall attend with sovereign care to establishing the passes and entries of the said Kingdom, and to inspecting the border regions of the neighboring [territories], and [removing people from] indefensible places and putting them into the castles and strongholds that are well defensible. Which castles and strongholds shall be provisioned with victuals, men-at-arms, and all other things necessary for their conservation and defense. And you shall keep all the land well warned and prepared, and in other manner take all those better expedients that you see fit, and collect and receive the men-at-arms who [come] for the protection and guard of the said Kingdom, and for the defense and good estate thereof, in such manner that it suffer no willing misfortune in the encounter.

[Let] the necessary provisions (rather let them be done with all diligence) [be made] as shall seem expedient to us.

Given in Barcelona under our secret seal, on the 26th day of July in the year 1389.

To our very dear brother, the Duke.

Most dear beloved and lady, inasmuch as I receive, as I ought, supreme pleasure and very great joy in learning of your good health and condition, and consequently with fervent and continual desire, I beseech you as affectionately as I can that you be willing to inform me of this clearly by your letters whenever you have opportunity. And since, most dear mother and lady, it likewise pleases you to know certain good tidings of my condition, I certify to you that I and my children, your grandchildren, are healthy and in good disposition of our persons, and that the convalescence of the lord King, my most dear husband and lord, continues from good to better, such that it is hoped he will be perfectly healed within a short time, God willing.

## 4. HISTORICAL NOTES

### Pierre de Luxembourg (1369–1387)
The "Cardinal of Luxembourg" referenced is almost certainly **Pierre de Luxembourg** (1369–1387), a young cardinal of the Avignon obedience who died at age 18 in July 1387 in Villeneuve-lès-Avignon. He was immediately reputed for sanctity, and miracles were reported at his tomb. His canonization process began almost immediately after his death.

**Connection to Violant de Bar**: Pierre de Luxembourg was related to the House of Luxembourg through the complex web of Franco-Imperial nobility. Violant de Bar (c. 1365–1431), daughter of Robert I of Bar and Marie of France, was connected to Luxembourg through her mother's Valois lineage and through marriages within the extended Luxembourg-Brabant-Valois network. The queen's reference to him as "consanguinei mei" (my kinsman) reflects these dynastic ties.

### Routier Companies from Castile
The reference to "companyes que tornats sen de Castella en ffran[ça]" reflects the ongoing problem of free companies (routiers) during the Hundred Years' War. These mercenary bands, often unemployed after campaigns, would traverse territories causing devastation. The specific reference to companies returning from Castile may relate to:
- Aftermath of the Castilian civil wars
- Mercenary bands that had served in the Peninsula returning to France
- The ongoing chaos following the Great Schism (1378)

### The Abbot of Osona
The recipient of Document 1 is identified as the abbot of Osona. This likely refers to one of the major monasteries in the county of Osona (modern Osona comarca in Catalonia), possibly:
- Sant Pere de Casserres
- Santa Maria de l'Estany
- Or another Benedictine/Augustinian foundation in the region

**Guillem de Copons**: A member of the Copons lineage, a prominent Catalan noble family with estates in the Conca de Barberà region. Served as royal envoy and trusted messenger (fider/feel) for the Crown. The use of both titles "feel e fider" (faithful and trusted) indicates his high standing as a diplomatic courier.

**King of Navarre**: In September 1389, this would be **Charles III "the Noble"** (r. 1387–1425), who had succeeded his father Charles II "the Bad" in January 1387. Charles III was related to the House of Aragon through multiple marriage alliances, explaining the kinship address "molt car e molt amat cosgerma" (very dear and very beloved cousin/brother-in-law). The term "cosgerma" (cossí germà) indicates close familial relationship.

Louis II was Queen Violant's maternal uncle — Violant was the daughter of Robert I, Duke of Bar, and Marie of France, whose mother was Bonne of Luxembourg. The family was deeply involved in Valencian factional politics, often in conflict with rival noble houses. This document suggests legal proceedings were underway against him and his properties, possibly related to jurisdictional disputes or political conflicts in the Kingdom of Valencia.

**Governor of Valencia (Governador d'Outra)**: The "Governador d'Outra el regne de València" was the royal governor with jurisdiction over the southern portion of the Kingdom of Valencia (beyond the Xúquer River), as opposed to the "Governador de ça" (citra) for the northern region. In 1389, this position was held by members of the high Valencian nobility.

The documents reveal coordination between King Joan I and Queen Violant in diplomatic and legal matters. The Queen's involvement in the Vilaragut case shows her active role in Valencian governance, while the joint credence letter demonstrates the royal couple's collaborative approach to Navarrese and French relations. The reference to proceeding "per lo fur" indicates the application of Valencian foral law (Furs de València) in the Vilaragut proceedings.

## 4. HISTORICAL NOTES

### Persons:

1. **Violant de Bar (c. 1365–1431):** Queen of Aragon as wife of Joan I (r. 1387–1396). Daughter of Robert I, Duke of Bar, and Marie of Valois. Known for her cultural patronage and political correspondence. This letter dates from the first year of her husband's reign.

2. **Édouard de Bar (d. 1415):** Younger brother of Violant de Bar; son of Robert I, Duke of Bar. The Queen was attempting to secure the bishopric of Uzès for him through papal provision. He later became Bishop of Verdun (1395–1415) and Metz (1394), and died at Agincourt.

3. **Joan I of Aragon (1350–1396):** "The Hunter" (el Caçador), King of Aragon 1387–1396. Referenced here as "lo senyor Rey nostre marit."

4. **Pope Clement VII (Robert of Geneva, r. 1378–1394):** The Avignon pope during the Western Schism. Aragon supported the Avignon papacy. This letter expresses Violant's frustration that despite the Crown of Aragon's loyalty, Clement VII did not grant the bishopric of Uzès to her brother.

### Places:

5. **Uzès:** Episcopal see in Languedoc (modern Gard, France). The bishopric was a significant benefice in the Avignonese orbit. The papal provision to someone other than Édouard de Bar caused this diplomatic complaint.

6. **Barcelona:** Location of the royal court; place of issue.

### Context:

This letter is an early expression of tension between the Aragonese crown and Pope Clement VII. Despite the Crown of Aragon's firm support for the Avignon papacy during the Western Schism (declared by Pere III in 1378 and maintained by Joan I), the Queen perceives that the Pope has not adequately rewarded their loyalty through ecclesiastical patronage for her family. The threat to "withdraw" (lexar) signals willingness to reconsider the relationship—a significant diplomatic statement given the schism context.

## 4. HISTORICAL NOTES

### Document 1

**King of Spain (Rey Despanya):** This refers to Juan I of Castile (1379-1390), whose illness and recovery is being reported. The designation "King of Spain" was sometimes used loosely for the Castilian monarch. Joan I of Aragon had close dynastic ties with Castile, and news of the Castilian king's health would have been politically significant.

**Cardinal of Viviers:** Jean de Brogny (c. 1342-1426), Cardinal of Viviers (created cardinal 1385), was a prominent figure in the Avignon papacy and later the Great Western Schism. He was a supporter of the Avignon line.

**Cardinal of Luxembourg:** Pierre de Luxembourg (1369-1387), Cardinal of San Giorgio in Velabro, died on 2 July 1387 at age 18. He was renowned for his extraordinary piety and asceticism. Immediately after his death, miracles were attributed to him, and his cult spread rapidly. He was beatified in 1527. The reference to his "life and miracles" indicates the early stages of his veneration, less than three months after his death.

**Marquis of Villena:** Alfonso d'Aragó "el Vell" (the Elder), Marquis of Villena and Count of Dénia (c. 1332-1412), was one of the most powerful nobles in the Crown of Aragon. He held extensive territories and was an important diplomat. His correspondence with Queen Violant suggests involvement in international affairs concerning the papacy.

**"Lo dret del papa de la Esgleya":** This refers to the contested legitimacy of the Avignon pope (Clement VII, 1378-1394) during the Great Western Schism. The Crown of Aragon supported the Avignon obedience, and the miracles of Pierre de Luxembourg were seen as divine confirmation of the Avignon pope's legitimacy.

### Document 2

**Castell de Palol:** Likely Palol de Revardit or a related settlement in the Girona region of Catalonia.

**Jews of Peratallada:** Peratallada (in the Baix Empordà, Girona) had a small Jewish community. This document records an armed attack ("aguayt e invasio") against Jews, consistent with patterns of anti-Jewish violence in late 14th-century Catalonia, particularly during periods of social and economic tension. The 1380s saw increasing hostility toward Jewish communities, culminating in the devastating pogroms of 1391.

**Governor of Catalonia:** The Governador General de Catalunya was one of the highest royal officials in the principality, with extensive judicial and administrative powers. At this time, the position may have been held by Ramon Alemany de Cervelló or a similar magnate.

**Legal procedure:** The queen's command for a personal inquisition (*jnquisicio*) and proceeding against the culprits and their goods (*procehiats contra los culpables e lurs bens*) reflects standard criminal procedure under royal jurisdiction for crimes against Jews, who were considered property of the Crown (*servi regis*).

The documents date from the early months of Joan I's reign (he succeeded Pere III in January 1387). **[To the most high and most excellent and most gracious prince and lord, husband and my most dear lord.]**

From your great lordship I have received a letter of yours most graciously [written], which, lord, I have received with very great pleasure and consolation, especially since through it I have learned of your good health, and [it is] very singularly growing. And for your safeguard, lord, [may] his divinity cause [you] to prosper for a long time, I pray that you, lord, and I [may meet] soon.

**Violant de Bar (Yolande de Bar)** (c. 1365–1431): Queen consort of Aragon as wife of Joan I (r. 1387–1396). Daughter of Robert I, Duke of Bar, and Marie of France. Known for her active role in court administration and cultural patronage.

**Margarita de Peralta, Countess of Caltabellotta and Caltanissetta**: A Sicilian noblewoman. The Peralta family were prominent in Aragonese Sicily. Caltabellotta and Caltanissetta were important Sicilian counties held by this lineage.

**Aznar Pardo de la Casta**: A Valencian nobleman who served as Governor (Governador) of the Kingdom of Valencia under Joan I. The Pardo de la Casta family were prominent in Valencian administration.

**Berenguer de Vilaragut**: A Valencian knight whose estate is the subject of Document B. The Vilaragut were a major noble lineage in the Kingdom of Valencia. The document suggests his widow's inheritance passed to the crown (likely through escheat or donation), and the queen is now asserting her rights against multiple claimants.

### Places

**Vilafranca del Penedès**: Town in Catalonia, frequently a residence of the royal court. The queen's itinerary in late 1387 places her here.

**Kingdom of Valencia**: One of the constituent realms of the Crown of Aragon, with its own governor and legal system.

**Caltabellotta / Caltanissetta**: Sicilian towns and counties, possessions of the Peralta family.

Lady Yolant, by the grace of God Queen of Aragon, etc., to the very noble and high Lord Abdorrefimen, by the same mercy of God King of Tlemcen Trimita, and of all its dependencies: greetings and the fullness of good friendship.

We have received your letter and the gifts which Mahomet ben Yaco Adai, your messenger, has presented to us on your behalf, for which we have had great pleasure, knowing that you wish to preserve the confederation and good friendship that has existed between the past Kings of Aragon and your predecessors, Kings of Trimite. And so it is today, and so it shall be, God willing, for all time between the lord King, our very dear husband and lord, and yourself, and consequently we are very grateful for this, urging you, noble King, as affectionately as we can, that you hold the subjects of the lord King and our own—merchants as well as others who trade and reside in your realm—as recommended out of reverence for the lord King and ourselves, and that you be willing to treat them as favorably as your own, for we likewise intend to do and shall do the same for yours, whom out of consideration and honor for you we would willingly please in whatever we might.

And wishing to respond to you in like manner and to honor [you] with our presents, we send to you by your said messenger, who returns to you, one mantle made according to the fashion now used in these parts, of figured 'poret' cloth. And we ask that you send us perfumes and silk cloths which, by their rarity, may please us as beautiful, and consequently we very much desire to have them. And if any of the beasts that carry the civet [algalia] come [to market], send us some likewise. Write to us about all things that you may wish of that which is given, for we shall comply with great pleasure, without any fail.

Given at Vilafranca on the 8th day of January of the year 1389. The Queen.

This document dates from less than a year after Joan I's accession (January 1387). This document cluster relates to the **coronation of King Joan I and Queen Violant de Bar**, which took place on **13 April 1388** in Zaragoza. The urgency expressed ("lo breu temps d[e]la coronacio[n]") reflects the January 1388 date, approximately three months before the ceremony. The Crown required substantial subsidies (*demandes*) from the kingdoms to fund the elaborate ceremonies.

1. **Bartomeu Sirvent** — Queen Violant's secretary (*secretari*), who administered her secret seal (*segell secret*). The register title confirms his role: "Registrum Curie mei Bartholomei Sirvent."

2. **Jacobus Pastoris / Jaume Pastor de Çaragoça** — A Zaragozan notable, likely a *ciutadà honrat* (honored citizen) or urban official involved in tax collection or liaison with royal administration. The family name Pastor/Pastoris appears in Zaragozan documentation of this period.

3. **Governor of Aragon** (*Gouernador d'Arago*) — In 1388, this office was likely held by **Juan Fernández de Heredia** or his lieutenant. The Governor was the Crown's chief judicial and administrative representative in the kingdom.

4. **Batlle General of Aragon** (*batle general*) — Royal fiscal officer responsible for collecting Crown revenues in the kingdom.

5. **Çerino de Çaragoça** — Likely the *Zalmedina* (from Arabic *ṣāḥib al-madīna*), the chief municipal magistrate of Zaragoza, a crucial figure for urban tax collection.

### Location
**Vilafranca** — Almost certainly **Vilafranca del Penedès**, a favored royal residence of Joan I and Violant, located in Catalonia. The royal household spent considerable time there in the late 1380s.

### Persons Identified

1. **Violant de Bar (Yolande of Bar)** - Queen consort of Aragon (1365-1431), wife of Joan I. These documents are issued under her secret seal as part of her household administration. She was known for active involvement in court affairs and had her own chancery operation.

2. **Sanxo de la Torre** - Royal *posador* (lodging-master/harbinger). This official was responsible for arranging lodgings in advance of royal visits. The position was crucial for itinerant medieval courts.

3. **"La Reyna Vella" (The Queen Dowager)** - This refers to **Sibil·la de Fortià** (c. 1350-1406), fourth wife of Pere III el Cerimoniós and stepmother of Joan I. After Pere III's death in January 1387, Sibil·la's position became precarious. Joan I initially confiscated her properties, and there were ongoing disputes about her dower and maintenance payments. 2. **Zaragoza** - Capital of Aragon; reference suggests financial matters connected to that city.

### Historical Context

The date of **June 1388** places these documents approximately 18 months into Joan I's reign (he succeeded Pere III on 5 January 1387). The references to lodging arrangements and the Queen Dowager's finances reflect:

- The itinerant nature of the Crown of Aragon court
- Ongoing negotiations regarding Sibil·la de Fortià's financial settlement
- The operational complexity of coordinating two queens' households (Violant and Sibil·la)

## HISTORICAL NOTES

### Persons

**Violant de Bar (c. 1365-1431):** Queen consort of Aragon as wife of Joan I (r. 1387-1396). Daughter of Robert I, Duke of Bar, and Marie of Valois. Known for her cultural patronage and political involvement. These letters date from early in her time as queen.

**Bartholomeus Sirvent:** Royal secretary (secretarius) to Queen Violant, responsible for documents under the secret seal (sigillum secretum). The register title confirms his role: "Registrum Curie mei Bartholomei Sirvent."

**Countess of Caltabellotta:** Likely Costanza Chiaramonte, wife of Guglielmo Peralta, Count of Caltabellotta in Sicily. The Peralta family were Aragonese nobles with extensive Sicilian holdings. The Chiaramonte were a powerful Sicilian family. This connection reflects the Crown of Aragon's ongoing involvement in Sicilian affairs.

**Vescomte de Rocabertí:** Likely Felip Dalmau II de Rocabertí (d. 1392), Vescomte de Rocabertí, who served in the royal administration. The Rocabertí were one of the most prominent noble families of Catalonia.

**Mossèn Guillem:** Chaplain serving as messenger/envoy for the Countess of Caltabellotta. The title "mossèn" (from "mon senyor") was used for clergy and knights in Catalan.

### Places

**Barcelona:** Primary residence of the Aragonese court during this period and location of chancery operations.

**Caltabellotta (Calatabillota):** Town and county in southwestern Sicily, site of the 1302 Peace of Caltabellotta that ended the War of the Sicilian Vespers. The county was held by the Peralta family, Aragonese nobles.

### Documentary Context

These three letters demonstrate the queen's independent diplomatic correspondence under her secret seal, distinct from the king's chancery. The letters follow similar formulae:
- Receipt of correspondent's letter
- Acknowledgment of credence delivered by messenger
- Promise of oral response through same messenger
- Standard dating clause with Barcelona, secret seal, day/month/year

The linguistic shift in Document 3 from Catalan to Aragonese/Castilian likely reflects the recipient's linguistic background or regional affiliation.

## 4. HISTORICAL NOTES

### Persons

**Marzarit Golluf** (*Marçarit Golluf* / *Margarito Golluf*): Queen Violant's treasurer and a trusted financial agent. The name "Golluf" suggests possible converso or Jewish family origins, common among Crown financial officers. His role as "Regens" indicates he may have been acting treasurer or holding additional administrative authority.

**Queen Violant de Bar** (*Yolans*): Wife of Joan I of Aragon (r. 1387–1396), daughter of Robert I, Duke of Bar, and Marie of Valois. She maintained her own household and treasury (*curia*), requiring separate financial administration. This document shows her actively managing substantial debts.

**King Joan I** (*Rex Johannes*): King of Aragon, Valencia, Mallorca, Sardinia, and Count of Barcelona from 1387. Son of Pere III (IV) "the Ceremonious."

**Pere III (IV) "the Ceremonious"** (*illustrissimi domini petri memorie recolende Regis Aragonum*): Deceased father of Joan I, died January 1387. The reference to debts owed by his court indicates the new reign was still settling accounts from the previous administration.

### Places

**Monastery of Valldonzella** (*monasterio Vallis Donzelle*): Cistercian convent founded 1237, located just outside Barcelona's medieval walls. The royal court frequently used religious houses for temporary residence. The convent still exists today in a different location in Barcelona.

### Financial Terminology

- **Mogubell / Remogubell**: Technical terms for compound interest, derived from Arabic *muqābala*. *Mogubell* refers to interest that compounds; *remogubell* to renewed or renegotiated compound interest. These terms are characteristic of Crown of Aragon financial documents.

- **Barata**: Exchange transaction, often involving currency conversion or commodity swap.

- **Comanda**: A type of deposit or commercial loan arrangement, from Latin *commenda*.

- **47,400 solidi barcelonenses**: A substantial sum. At roughly 12 diners per solidus and approximately 11 solidi per florin, this represents roughly 4,300 gold florins—a significant treasury operation.

### Context

This document reflects the chronic financial difficulties of the Crown of Aragon in the late fourteenth century. Queen Violant needed to raise approximately 47,400 solidi urgently for unspecified "necessary affairs" of her court. The authorization to borrow from Jews (*a quibuscumque personis seu judeis*) and at compound interest (*mogubell*) indicates the urgency and the willingness to accept unfavorable terms. The reference to collecting debts owed by both the current king's court and the late king's court suggests the Crown itself was both debtor and creditor in a complex web of obligations.

## 3. ENGLISH TRANSLATION

### Document 1

**[Address:]** Nephew

Very dear and very beloved, We [write] because we receive very great pleasure in knowing of your health and good estate; we ask that you would certify us of it every time that you have opportunity to do so. And believing that it similarly pleases you to know of us, we notify you that the Lord King our husband and our very dear lord, and we together with all our infantes, are healthy and in good disposition of our persons, thanks be to God. And if other things please you, very dear [nephew], from these parts hither, send to tell us and we shall fulfill them willingly. May [God's] mercy [and] the Holy Trinity guard you for all times. Given in Barcelona under our privy seal on the 18th day of April of the year 1388. The Queen.

**[Subscription:]** It was directed thus: To our very dear and very beloved brother Don Enrique, Primogenito of Castile.

**[Chancery note:]** The Lady Queen commanded [this] to me, Bartolomé Sirvent.

Very dear and much beloved cousin,

We have received your letters and understood them through the account that was explained and heard through Lord Thomas de Copines, your counselor. It would seem that you would not wish [to proceed with] the marriage of the Infanta, our daughter, and of our very dear son the Dauphin, for if you had wished it, you would have had to give [consent] so that when the Infanta was in our power, the other things that we were obligated to follow and fulfill according to the form of the agreement made thereon would be completed through action.

And as to the fact that [you] cannot do so, we are greatly astonished that you are [raising?] many matters that need not be explained at present — matters which, in our judgment, should reasonably move us and render [us] affectionate, so that we might affectionately never make known your clear and final intention at present, which we should have known by Saint John's Day [24 June] past.

Likewise, we are astonished at what was [communicated] through the said Lord Thomas in favor of Bourg or Villaregut, concerning how [he] raised the matter, and because it was very grievous and displeasing that you would incline in favor [of the accused?], you ought not to have intervened, but rather [allowed] that grievous punishment be inflicted as is fitting. For according to what we know, the said deed touched the person of the Lord King, [our] very dear husband and lord, and ourselves, and we are aggrieved so greatly that more is not possible. And from this and similar [offenses] we intend, as we ought, that whatever charges arise, due correction shall be made.

And we wish you to know this, and that you understand it thus. And in doing the above-said and against others who appear in the household of the Lord King, you have proceeded [?] according to true justice and proper order and law — which justice could not [be served?] otherwise, and in the said Bourg [matter] with [suspended?] favors and blandishments. And thus do not have [any] displeasure, whether it be displeasing to your [interests?] or not, for we could not properly do [otherwise] for you, nor do you owe [us] to [do so].

Concerning the matter of the clerics and of your [beneficed clergy?] in the person of the Lord King — that is, that they should be admitted to benefices — we have instantly supplicated the said lord on your honor's behalf, and he has responded, and it is true that he will fulfill [this]. And you [should] deign [to do] other things, and henceforth for the good state of this [realm?], it has been deliberately proposed that no foreigner should be admitted to any benefice [nor?] intends to do so through his [authority?] immutably, with all exceptions, especially since one has nullly obtained the apprehension thereof.

Wherefore, very dear cousin, hold us in this as reasonably obligated to duty. And thus if other things please [you] that we may do for your honor, entrust [them?] to us with full confidence. May the Holy Trinity guard you always. Given at Zaragoza under our secret seal on the [...] day of August. The Queen.

### Document 2: Letter of Condolence

**Most dear King and most beloved brother:** We, the Queen of Aragon, send you great salutations, as one through whom we desire that God give you as much health and honor as you yourself desire. 

Know, most dear royal brother, that we received your good letter, and having understood it and the things that Fray Toribio, Custodian of the Friars Minor of Palencia, your familiar, has told us most discreetly and well on your behalf, we firmly believe that you—both for the reasons set forth in your letter and also because of your pious humanity—have shared and continue to share with us the great transcendent sorrow that we had and have from the death of our most dear son, the Dauphin.

And this, and the most pure and sound counsel that you give us—which, although we are well [aware] that we can [follow it], from your very great and famous [advice]—we thank you as much as we are able. However, we cannot make good use of it yet, since through our frailty, the constraining law of nature does not permit us to find consolation from such a great and grievous loss.

For all, may our Lord God be praised, whom may it please, through His infinite mercy, that He may henceforth give us that consolation which we need, and keep us in His holy grace perpetually.

And if there are any things that we can [do] for you, most dear brother, for your honor, send [word] telling us of them, and we shall fulfill them with all our heart.

And may the Holy Trinity be your guardian at all times. Given at Zaragoza under our secret seal on the 11th day of September of the year 1388.

## 4. HISTORICAL NOTES

### Persons Identified

1. **Johan de Montros** (Johannes de Montros): Designated as *receptor et distributor* (receiver and distributor) of the papal camera's portion. This appears to be a royal official of Joan I serving as intermediary for papal revenues. The name "Montros" could be a variant of Montroig or similar Catalan toponymic.

2. **The Abbot ("dictus abbas")**: Named on the previous folio; appointed as sub-collector working alongside the main Apostolic Collector. Abbots frequently served in this capacity due to their ecclesiastical standing and administrative experience.

### Institutional Context

- **Apostolic Camera** (*camera apostolica*): The papal financial administration. Under the Avignon papacy and subsequent schism, complex arrangements were needed to collect revenues in kingdoms recognizing each obedience.

- **Annates** (*annatae*): Fees paid to the papacy upon appointment to benefices, typically the first year's revenue. A major source of papal income.

- **Medietatem nostram**: The "half" referenced indicates a revenue-sharing arrangement between the papacy and the Crown of Aragon—common in this period where kings negotiated portions of ecclesiastical revenues.

- **Racional/Rational**: The *Mestre Racional* was the chief auditor of the Crown of Aragon, responsible for reviewing all financial accounts.

- **Albarà** (*albarana*): A receipt or voucher document, borrowed from Arabic *al-barā'a*. Standard term in Aragonese-Catalan financial administration.

### Historical Significance

This document illustrates the complex financial cooperation between the Avignon papacy and the Crown of Aragon during the Western Schism (1378-1417). Queen Violant de Bar, herself French and connected to the Avignon obedience through her family, was instrumental in maintaining this relationship. The copying of this papal letter into her *Curie Sigilli Secreti* register indicates her personal involvement in administering these arrangements.

## 3. ENGLISH TRANSLATION

### First Document

**The Queen**

Viscountess: We have received your letter. And the dispute displeases us so much that it could not displease us more, saying thus about how great [a matter it is] that the King of France [is in conflict] with the Dukes of Jülich and of Guelders, especially as the matter comes to battle. According to what is arranged concerning the deeds of arms, as the outcomes of great battles are very uncertain—and such that there is no remedy—consequently, as far as is possible, we would do everything lawful so that the battle might cease and the dispute be lifted amicably and finally. May it please Our Lord God that He might provide a salutary remedy [so that] they might pass through it in a more honest manner.

And we ask you and wish that whether battle follows or not, you make known to us the matter at length: what will have happened, and how many or which [persons] will have been there, and all the circumstances, according to what shall seem fitting to do. For we shall not be without great anxiety and perplexity until we have certain good news of it.

Concerning the matter of the King of Navarre, what you have made known to us displeases us greatly. And we well believe that if [he] had followed our intention or counsel, it would have turned out well. Because it is given to silence before [?]. It pleases us greatly that all the daughters of our very dear uncle the Duke of Burgundy are placed [in marriage] in the manner you have notified, that with other prosperities there is such affection as if they were properly our [own] daughters.

And because now you are not needed here, but are very necessary [there], and because the King, at our instant supplication, has granted the General Corts of Aragon—already in fact convoked for the third Thursday of November approaching, at Monzón—come back immediately, all delay cast aside, as it would be expedient that you both be here already, as much for the reason of the said Corts as for other things, according to what the lord King has already written to you. And then, when you are here, we shall discuss fully the matter of the marriage.

Given at Zaragoza under our small seal, on the 19th day of September of the year 1388. The Queen.

## 4. HISTORICAL NOTES

### Persons

**The Viscountess of Rocabertí and Roda:** This is almost certainly **Beatriu de Cabrera** (fl. 1370s–1400s), who held the viscounties of Rocabertí and Roda through her marriage to Vescomte Dalmau VII de Rocabertí. She was a trusted diplomatic agent of Queen Violant and frequently served as an intermediary with the French court, given her connections and linguistic abilities. The letter addresses her in Paris, where she was apparently serving as the queen's representative.

**The King of France:** Charles VI (r. 1380–1422), who was indeed in conflict with the Dukes of Jülich and Guelders in 1388, part of the complex Brabantine succession disputes.

**The Dukes of Jülich and Guelders:** William I, Duke of Guelders (also Duke of Jülich from 1393), was involved in territorial conflicts with French interests in the Low Countries during this period. The "battle" mentioned may refer to military actions related to these disputes.

**The King of Navarre:** Charles II "the Bad" of Navarre (r. 1349–1387) had died on 1 January 1387. By September 1388, his successor Charles III was on the throne. The reference to displeasure about the King of Navarre likely concerns ongoing diplomatic matters with the new king or unresolved issues from the previous reign.

**The Duke of Burgundy:** Philip the Bold (1342–1404), Duke of Burgundy, was Queen Violant's uncle (her mother, Marie de France, was Philip's sister). The marriages of his daughters were matters of high dynastic importance:
- Margaret married William of Bavaria (future Count of Hainaut)
- Catherine married Leopold IV of Austria
- Mary married Amadeus VIII of Savoy
- Bonne married future count of Nevers

**The Corts of Aragon at Monzón:** Joan I convoked the General Corts at Monzón for late 1388. The "third Thursday of November" would fall around 15-21 November 1388.

### The Postscript — "King of Spain"

The postscript contains highly problematic historical content. The reference to "the King of Spain" (*lo Rey d'espona*) dying without male heir and the King of France being made heir, with implications for the King of England, does not correspond to any known event of 1388.

1. **Scribal error or confusion:** The scribe may have garbled news about succession disputes elsewhere
2. **"Espona/Espoina" as garbled toponym:** This may refer to a different realm entirely—perhaps a miscopying of news about Brittany, Scotland, or another duchy
3. **Speculative diplomatic intelligence:** The viscountess may have been reporting rumors circulating in Paris that proved unfounded

This passage requires further investigation. The Castilian king in 1388 was Juan I (d. 1390), who had male heirs.

## 4. HISTORICAL NOTES

### Document 1

1. **Joan Ferràndiç d'Urries**: A nobleman from the Aragonese lineage of Urries, serving as royal envoy. The Urries family held lands in upper Aragon and served frequently in diplomatic capacities.

2. **Tàrrega and Vilagrassa**: Towns in the county of Urgell (modern Lleida province). These were subject to jurisdictional disputes between the Crown and the Duke of Montblanc.

3. **Duke of Montblanc**: This is the Infante Martí (the future King Martí I), brother of King Joan I. He held the duchy of Montblanc from 1387. The reference to him as "molt car frare" (very dear brother) of Queen Violant is a courtesy extension—he was actually her brother-in-law.

4. **Context**: This letter thanks the citizens of Lleida for remitting legal proceedings against residents of Tàrrega and Vilagrassa who were vassals of the Duke of Montblanc, suggesting an inter-jurisdictional conflict resolved through royal intervention.

### Document 2

1. **Mossèn Lur de Bonastre**: Likely a member of the Bonastre lineage from Catalonia, serving as courier/messenger for the Marchioness.

2. **Falcon request**: Falcons were prestige gifts in medieval courts. This letter reveals the complex gift economy: the Queen could not secure a particular falcon because the King had already promised it to another noble (Epime Peç d'Arenós).

3. **Arenós family**: The lords of Arenós (Arenós de Ribagorza) were an important Aragonese noble lineage. "Epime" may be a scribal rendering of "Eiximè" or "Jaume."

4. **Marchioness of Villena**: If the directio reading is correct, this would be Juana Manuel, or possibly another member of the Villena marquisate family. The Marquisate of Villena was held at this time by Alfonso of Aragon, grandson of Jaume II. The recipient may be his wife or a female relative.

5. **"Lo pont perdut"**: This phrase is obscure. It may refer to a specific bridge or toll right, or be a metaphorical expression. Alternatively, it could be a scribal error for "lo pont [a]perdut" (the bridge prepared/ready).

## 4. HISTORICAL NOTES

### Persons

1. **Queen Violant de Bar (Yolande of Bar)** (c. 1365-1431): Wife of Joan I of Aragon, daughter of Robert I, Duke of Bar. The references to her pregnancy ("sia prenys") are significant—she bore several children during this period, though many died in infancy.

2. **Pere de Berga**: A procurator or envoy sent by the queen to the papal curia. He appears throughout this folio and the preceding one, indicating he was the designated agent for these petitions to the pope.

3. **Madona Carroça (Lady Carroça)**: Likely **Carroça de Vilaragut**, a prominent Valencian noblewoman who was a favorite of Joan I and a controversial figure at court. She was accused of wielding excessive influence and was eventually implicated in accusations of witchcraft.

4. **"Lo senyor Rey"**: Joan I of Aragon (r. 1387-1396).

5. **"Lo papa" / "sant pare"**: The papal reference during this period would be to either **Urban VI** (Roman obedience, r. 1378-1389) or **Clement VII** (Avignonese obedience, r. 1378-1394). The Crown of Aragon initially remained neutral in the Schism but eventually supported Avignon under Benedict XIII.

### Institutions

1. **Order of Tortosa / Order of Montesa**: The military Order of Montesa, founded in 1317 by Jaume II of Aragon from the assets of the suppressed Templars, headquartered in the Kingdom of Valencia. The queen's "gran devocio" to this order is documented.

2. **Papal Curia**: The petitions concern obtaining papal bulls and graces—standard diplomatic activity for a queen consort seeking spiritual privileges and political favors.

### Concepts

- **"Rotol de gracies"**: A rotulus or roll listing multiple petitions to be submitted to the papal chancellery for approval and signing.
- **"Bulls"**: Papal documents sealed with the *bulla* (lead seal); these required fees (the "quantitat necessaria" mentioned).
- **"Compare" (godfather/co-parent)**: The spiritual kinship through baptism was significant in medieval society.

Dear cousin,

We have received your letter. Having understood its contents and what lord Pere de Navallès has told us on your behalf, we thank you greatly for your good offer, which, in case it were necessary, the lord King and we would accept. And in other manner we would accompany you in all that pertains to our benefit and honor, as one of whom we hold high esteem. We believe for certain what [is fitting] for a good friend or [what] concerns you.

Regarding what they have given [you] to understand: there is no basis for it, nor will there be in the future, God willing. And we believe that the subjects of the lord King are not in any discord with him, but rather [they] hope firmly, trusting in their innate naturalness and cordial affection which they have always shown and show to their King and lord.

And considering the sound intention of the lord King, the general Corts which the said lord is celebrating will have within a short time such a concordant conclusion that it will be pleasing to God and will result in great service to the lord King and to us, and [to] the good estate of his Kingdoms and lands.

Furthermore, know, dear cousin, that we have petitioned the said lord with great insistence that he send the white jennet, and we could not obtain it—and because this matter, which need not be forced, we could not do properly—but condescending now to our supplication, the said lord sends you [a horse named] Corvello, as he informs you by his letter.

And if there are other things you wish, dear cousin, that we can do, write to us with full confidence. And may the Holy Spirit guard you.

Given at Monzón under our secret seal, on the 18th day of November of the year 1388. The Queen.

## 4. HISTORICAL NOTES

### Persons

**Louis de Sancerre** (c. 1340–1402): Marshal of France from 1369, not actually a viscount. The title "vescomte de ffrança" may be a scribal error or an informal designation. He was a prominent French military commander during the Hundred Years' War.

**Pere de Navallès**: A Catalan noble who served as an intermediary and messenger between the Aragonese court and the Count of Foix. He appears frequently in the queen's correspondence of this period.

**Count of Foix**: At this date, this is **Mathieu de Castelbon** (r. 1391–1398) or more likely his predecessor **Gaston III "Fébus"** (r. 1343–1391), the famous count and author. Gaston Fébus was related to the Aragonese royal house through marriage connections, hence the address "car cosí" (dear cousin).

**Jean, Duke of Berry** (1340–1416): Third son of King Jean II of France, famous patron of the arts and bibliophile. He was indeed the maternal uncle of Violant de Bar—Violant's mother, Marie de France, was Jean's sister. The duke's legendary book collection included many illuminated manuscripts.

**"Guillermos de Mexant"**: This appears to be a reference to **Guillaume de Machaut** (c. 1300–1377), the celebrated French poet and composer. The phonetic spelling "Mexant" for "Machaut" is consistent with medieval Catalan/Occitan pronunciation. This is a significant reference to literary culture and book exchange among the high nobility.

### Places

**Monzón** (Montso/Oçontso): A strategically important town in Aragon where the royal court frequently resided. The Corts of Aragon, Catalonia, and Valencia were sometimes held there. Joan I was convening the General Corts at Monzón during this period (1388–1389).

### Events

**The General Corts of 1388–1389**: This letter references Joan I's convocation of the Corts General at Monzón. The queen's optimistic language about a "concordant conclusion" reflects the tense political negotiations of this assembly, which dealt with taxation, jurisdictional disputes, and the king's controversial policies.

**The White Jennet**: A jennet (*ginet*) was a small Spanish horse prized for its smooth gait. White horses were particularly valuable and often exchanged as diplomatic gifts. The queen's failed attempt to obtain this horse and the substitution of "Corvello" (possibly a horse's name, meaning "little crow" or dark horse) illustrates the complex gift economy of medieval diplomacy.

### Persons

1. **Violant de Bar (Yolande of Bar)** (c. 1365–1431): Queen consort of Aragon as wife of Joan I. Daughter of Robert I, Duke of Bar, and Marie of France. She was the niece of Charles V of France, making Charles VI her cousin ("our very dear brother the King of France" reflects the diplomatic courtesy language).

2. **Joan I of Aragon** ("lo senyor Rey"): King of Aragon 1387–1396, husband of Violant de Bar.

3. **Charles VI of France** ("lo Rey de ffrança"): King of France 1380–1422. The reference to him as "our very dear brother" (car frare) uses conventional diplomatic kinship terminology.

4. **The Count of Foix** ("lo Comte de ffoix"): Gaston III Fébus (1331–1391), Count of Foix and Viscount of Béarn. A crucial figure in Pyrenean politics, he maintained complex relationships with both the French and Aragonese crowns. His territory straddled the border, making his allegiance strategically vital.

5. **Mossèn Bureu de la Ribera**: A French ambassador/envoy sent by Charles VI to negotiate with the Count of Foix. The name "Bureu" may be a Catalanized form of "Bureau" or similar French surname.

### Places

- **Monzón (Montçó)**: Town in Aragon where the Corts Generals of the Crown of Aragon were frequently held. The royal court was present here in February 1388–1389, likely for parliamentary sessions.

### Historical Context

The third document reflects the complex Franco-Aragonese diplomacy of the late 1380s. After the Great Schism (1378), France supported the Avignon papacy while Aragon initially recognized Rome. Joan I's reign saw efforts to improve relations with France, partly through his marriage to Violant de Bar. The negotiations with the Count of Foix were crucial for securing the Pyrenean frontier and maintaining peace between the two kingdoms. The language suggests efforts to bring Foix firmly into the French diplomatic orbit while maintaining his good relations with Aragon—a delicate balancing act.

> To the most excellent and powerful prince, most dear and most beloved brother. Know that the Marquis of Villena, your cousin and ours, desiring to recover and have [returned] his son Don Alfonso, who has been held prisoner in England for a long time for a certain sum of money for his ransom—for which [sum] he has newly agreed and negotiated with the Duke of Lancaster that the said Don Alfonso shall come to Bordeaux or to Bayonne with your safe-conduct, which the said Marquis has promised and is obligated to obtain—and since the lord King, our most dear husband and lord, who writes to you regarding this matter, has very great affection for the deliverance of the said Don Alfonso, as is proper, and we no less [affection], we cordially beseech you, most dear brother, that you be pleased, for the honor of the lord King and ours, and in consideration of the good kinship that the said Marquis has with us and with the lord King and with us, to liberally grant the said safe-conduct, valid for two years counting from its date forward—not only to the said Don Alfonso, but also to the ship or vessel that shall carry him, and to all those who shall come in the said ship or vessel, and to their goods—as fully and sufficiently as can be done. And [we ask] that you be pleased to have it delivered to the bearer of this present [letter], who goes there for this reason. By this, most dear and most beloved brother, you will do great pleasure to the lord King and to us, for which we shall be most grateful to you. And if any matters from these parts please you, write to us about them with full confidence, for we shall fulfill them with great heart. And may the holy divinity be your guardian always. ## 4. HISTORICAL NOTES

### The Royal Birth
This document records the birth of **Infante Jaume** (James), born to King Joan I and Queen Violant de Bar on the night of **24-25 March 1389** at **Monzón** (Montsó in Catalan), where the Corts of Aragon were being held. The infant was heir to the throne but died young (probably 1390), never reigning. This birth announcement is of significant historical value for documenting the exact circumstances.

### Recipients of Document B
The letter is addressed to the "Duke of Berry" - **Jean de France, duc de Berry** (1340-1416), uncle of King Charles VI of France and brother-in-law of Robert I, Duke of Bar. This was part of Violant's strategy of maintaining close ties with the French royal family.

The five copies noted in the chancery direction went to:
1. **Robert I, Duke of Bar** (d. 1411) - Violant's father
2. **Marie de France, Countess/Duchess of Bar** (d. 1404) - Violant's mother, daughter of King Jean II of France
3. **The Queen [of France]** - Likely Isabeau of Bavaria, wife of Charles VI, though possibly a scribal reference to the Queen of Aragon's mother
4. **Henry of Bar and Marie de Coucy** - Violant's brother and his wife
5. **Philip of Bar** - Another of Violant's brothers

### Persons in Subscriptions
- **Bartolomeu Sirvent**: Chief secretary of Queen Violant's chancery, named in the register's title
- **Fernandus de Pace** (Ferran de Pau): Knight, councillor, and majordomo mentioned in Document A's subscription
- **Thomas** and **P[etrus]**: Register scribes who executed the copies

### Location
**Monzón** (Montsó): Town in Aragon where the Corts were convened. The royal court was present here during the first months of 1389.

## 4. HISTORICAL NOTES

### Persons

**Violant de Bar (Yolande of Bar)** (c. 1365–1431): Queen consort of Aragon as wife of Joan I. Daughter of Robert I, Duke of Bar. Known for her political acumen and cultural patronage. These letters date from early in her tenure as queen.

**The infant mentioned**: The son referenced in these documents is **Infant Jaume** (James), born 25 March 1389 (as confirmed by the preceding folio 141r). He would die in childhood (1390), one of several children Joan I and Violant lost.

**Bartolomeu Sirvent**: The queen's secretary (*secretarius*) who maintained this register. His name appears in the register's title and as scribe of these documents.

**Francesc Eiximenis (Eiximenio)**: (c. 1330–1409) The famous Franciscan writer and theologian, author of *Lo Crestià* and other major works. His appearance in the marginal note (as "Eximi[nii]" or "Eximinu") is significant – he had close ties to the Aragonese royal court and was a spiritual advisor. **Bernat de Camporrells**: A courtier or messenger serving as intermediary between the queen and the unidentified "cousin" (likely a noble relative).

### Places

**Monzón (Monço)**: Royal town in Aragon, site of a major castle and frequent location of the Aragonese Cortes. The royal court was evidently based here in spring 1388–1389.

**Scala Dei (Escaladei)**: The first Carthusian monastery in the Iberian Peninsula, founded 1194 in the Priorat region near Tarragona. A major royal foundation with close ties to the Crown of Aragon.

**Portaceli**: Carthusian monastery near Valencia, founded 1272. Another important royal Carthusian foundation.

**Sant Pol del Maresme**: Town on the Catalan coast; likely refers to a religious house there.

The documents reveal the queen performing typical royal devotional and ceremonial duties:
1. Announcing the birth of an heir to religious communities
2. Inviting ecclesiastical dignitaries to serve as baptismal sponsors (*compares*)
3. Maintaining diplomatic correspondence with relatives

The emphasis on Carthusian monasteries reflects the special devotion the Crown of Aragon showed to this order.

### Document 2

"The Queen.

Since for [a certain] cause we wish to know whether from the rights of the seals of the lady Queen our mother, whom God keep, there was deducted or given a tithe or any contribution, [we command] you that you certify us clearly of this matter by your letter, both concerning the time when you were her procurator and concerning the time of your predecessors, as much as can be known, with all diligence, in such manner that we may have it promptly. It was directed to Ferrario Çayoll, goldsmith of Barcelona.

[Subscription:] Bartholomeus Siruent [made this] by mandate of the lady Queen, through Francesc d'Arada, knight, who [spoke] of this with her [while she was] present, and she saw it.

## 4. HISTORICAL NOTES

### Persons

**Queen Violant de Bar (1365–1431):** Issuer of both documents. Queen consort of Aragon as wife of Joan I, daughter of Robert I, Duke of Bar, and Marie of Valois. Known for her active role in court administration and cultural patronage.

**Countess of Urgell (Document 1 recipient):** Most likely **Margalida de Montferrat** (d. 1418), wife of Count Pere II d'Urgell. The reference to her pregnancy and previous visit to court during a pregnancy provides valuable prosopographical data about her childbearing history.

**"La senyora Reyna nostra mare" (Document 2):** This refers to **Eleanor of Sicily (1325–1375)**, third wife of Pere III "el Cerimoniós" and mother of Joan I. She was noted for her administrative acumen and held various rights and properties, including apparently the Albufera of Valencia.

**Ferrario Çayoll / Ferrer Sayol (Document 2 recipient):** A goldsmith (*aurifaber*) of Barcelona who apparently served as procurator for Queen Eleanor of Sicily's seal rights. The fact that a goldsmith held this role is notable—goldsmiths often had charge of seals due to their role in manufacturing and maintaining them.

**Francesc d'Arada:** A knight (*miles*) serving in the queen's household, who transmitted her oral mandate to the secretary.

**Bartholomeus Siruent:** The queen's secretary, responsible for the *Curia Sigilli Secreti* register. His subscription confirms he drafted this document.

### Places

**Montçó (Monzón):** Town in Aragon, site of important Corts generals. The royal family was evidently there in late March 1387-1388, likely for parliamentary sessions.

**L'Albufera de València:** The famous coastal lagoon south of Valencia, an important royal property with fishing and hunting rights. The queen's inquiry about Eleanor of Sicily's title to this property suggests an inheritance question or potential dispute.

### Institutional Context

**Seal Rights (*drets dels segells*):** Medieval chanceries derived income from fees charged for sealing documents. The queen is investigating whether a tithe (*decima*) or contribution was ever levied on the seal fees of Queen Eleanor's household—this may relate to ecclesiastical or royal claims on chancery revenues.

**The General Court (Cort General):** The reference to the Countess's previous attendance at a *cort general* to visit King Pere III ("the lord King our father") places this visit before Pere's death in January 1387.

5. **The "P." mark at conclusion:** Likely a notarial validation mark. Could stand for *probatum* (approved), *placet* (it pleases), or be the initial of a reviewing official.

6. **Document 2 year date:** I am confident in reading "viiº" (1388) rather than "viiiij" (1389), but this should be verified against other documents in the register from this period for scribal dating patterns.

>

## HISTORICAL NOTES

### Persons

**Violant de Bar (Yolanda of Bar)** (c. 1365–1431): Queen consort of Aragon as wife of Joan I. Daughter of Robert I, Duke of Bar, and Marie of France. Known for her active role in administration and patronage. This register (Curie Sigilli Secreti) records her personal correspondence under her secret seal.

**Guerau de Queralt**: Noble envoy of the queen. The Queralt lineage was a prominent Catalan noble family with domains in the county of Barcelona. Served as diplomatic courier for sensitive missions.

**Mathieu de Castelbon, Count of Foix** (r. 1382–1391): Count of Foix and Viscount of Béarn. The "dear cousin" (*car cosí*) address reflects actual kinship ties between the royal houses of Aragon and the counts of Foix through multiple marriage alliances.

**Governor of Aragon**: The *Gubernator Aragonum* was the chief royal administrative officer for the kingdom of Aragon proper (as distinct from Catalonia or Valencia). In 1388, this was likely **Juan Jiménez Cerdán** or his immediate successor.

### Jewish Communities (*Aljamas*)

The document references the queen's revenues from Jewish *aljamas* (self-governing Jewish communities) in Aragon. Following the devastating pogroms of 1348 and continuing fiscal pressures, many *censales* (annuity contracts) owed by these communities had become "dead" (*muertos*)—i.e., the obligors had died or the communities had declined to the point of non-payment. The queen was attempting to recover these revenues, which formed part of her personal income (*camera reginalis*).

### Place

**Monzón**: Important town in Aragon, site of the castle of Monzón (former Templar stronghold). The royal court frequently resided here during sessions of the Aragonese Cortes. The May 1388 dating places this during a period when Joan I and Violant were actively managing the kingdom following Joan's accession in January 1387.

### Context:
These documents reflect the chronic financial pressures faced by the Crown of Aragon in the late 14th century. The queen is essentially mortgaging future tax revenues from the Jewish community to raise immediate funds, using the mechanism of census sales with redemption rights. The coordination between king and queen, and the use of multiple officials (Governor and Merino), suggests a significant financial operation requiring careful legal execution.

## 4. HISTORICAL NOTES

### Persons

**Queen Violant de Bar (Yolande of Bar)** (c. 1365–1431): Consort of Joan I of Aragon, daughter of Robert I, Duke of Bar. She was known for her cultural patronage and active involvement in governance. This register (Curie Sigilli Secreti) contains documents issued under her privy seal through her secretary Bartomeu Sirvent.

**Joan I of Aragon ("lo senyor Rey")** (1350–1396): King of Aragon from 1387. The mention of his tertian fever (a type of malaria with recurring fevers every other day) is historically significant as it documents the king's health during the Corts of Monzón.

**Count of Foix ("Comiti Fuxensis," "car cosí")**: Most likely **Mathieu de Castelbon** (d. 1398), Count of Foix from 1391 (and previously Viscount of Castelbon). The kinship term "cosí" (cousin) reflects the complex dynastic connections between the houses of Aragon, Bar, and Foix. The Count of Foix held lands straddling the Pyrenees and was a significant ally/vassal of the Crown of Aragon.

**Pere Johannis**: An official or servant of the Crown, temporarily in Valencia. The urgency of the summons suggests he held an important administrative role during the parliamentary session.

**Mossèn Francesc de Pau**: A knight (the title "mossèn" indicates knighthood) who was apparently in the service or circle of the Count of Foix. His illness prevented him from being placed at the Count's disposal for some unspecified service.

**Guillem de Maupaut (Maupas?)**: Author or owner of "lo liber molt bell" — the beautiful book sent by the Count of Foix. This could refer to a literary work or illuminated manuscript. The queen's practice of borrowing and returning books reflects the court's bibliophilic culture.

### Places

**Monzón (Montçó)**: Site of the Corts Generals (General Cortes) of the Crown of Aragon in 1388–1389. The royal couple was resident there for extended parliamentary sessions. Both documents are dated from Monzón.

**Valencia**: Location of Pere Johannis, summoned to return to the court at Monzón.

**Barcelona**: Mentioned as the destination for Francesc de Pau's medical treatment.

### Context

The Corts of Monzón (1388–1389) were significant assemblies convened early in Joan I's reign. The king's illness (tertian fever) documented here adds to our knowledge of his health problems, which would continue throughout his reign. The register's date range (1387–1390) corresponds to the transitional period following Pere III's death (January 1387) and the establishment of Joan I's government.

## 4. HISTORICAL NOTES

### Persons:
1. **Mossèn Eimeric / Eimeric de Sanullis** - Likely Godofre Eimeric or a member of the Eimeric family serving as chamberlain (camarlenc) to the Crown. The title "Mossèn" indicates knightly status.

2. **King of France ("nos frave molt car lo Rey de ffrança")** - Charles VI of France (r. 1380-1422), who was indeed Queen Violant de Bar's nephew through her sister Marie de Bar. The reference to his planned visit to Avignon in June 1389 is historically significant.

3. **The Infante** - Likely refers to the Infante Fernando (the future Fernando I of Aragon, "de Antequera"), who was firstborn son of Joan I and Violant de Bar, though he died young. Alternatively, this may refer to Infante Martí (the future Martí I).

4. **Bartolomeu/Bertran Sirvent** - The queen's secretary (secretari) who registered these documents, as indicated in the register's title.

5. **"d[omi]n[u]s dux"** - The Duke, likely referring to the Duke of Girona or another member of the royal family who co-signed the previous document.

### Places:
1. **Monzón (Monçoo)** - Important town in Aragon, site of a castle and frequent location of Corts (parliamentary assemblies). The royal court was evidently there in June 1389.

2. **Avignon (Avinyo)** - Seat of the Avignon Papacy and important diplomatic center. Charles VI's planned visit would have been a major political event.

3. **Beaucaire (Basçers)** - Town in Languedoc on the Rhône, near Avignon. A logical staging point for the French king's entourage preparing for the Avignon visit.

### Historical Context:
The urgency of Document 1 and the reference to Charles VI's visit to Avignon reflects the complex diplomacy of the Western Schism period (1378-1417). The Crown of Aragon under Joan I was navigating between the Avignon and Roman obediences, and Charles VI's movements would have been of great interest.

## 4. HISTORICAL NOTES

### Persons Identified:

1. **Queen Violant de Bar (Yolande de Bar)** (c. 1365–1431): Queen consort of Aragon as wife of Joan I. Daughter of Robert I, Duke of Bar, and Marie de France. The issuer of both documents.

2. **Marie de France, Countess of Bar** (1344–1404): Mother of Queen Violant, daughter of King Jean II of France. Recipient of Document 2. The address "mare" (mother) and the intimate salutation confirm the relationship.

3. **"Lo Rey de ffrança" (King of France)**: Charles VI of France (r. 1380–1422), described as Queen Violant's "molt car frare" (very dear brother). Charles VI was indeed her cousin (both were grandchildren of Jean II of France), but "frare" was commonly used for close male relatives in diplomatic correspondence.

4. **"Lo Rey d'anglaterra" (King of England)**: Richard II of England (r. 1377–1399). The reference to his crossing suggests Anglo-French diplomatic tensions that might delay Charles VI's movements.

5. **"Lo pare sant" (the Holy Father)**: This refers to **Clement VII** (Avignon papacy, r. 1378–1394), as the Crown of Aragon recognized the Avignon obedience during the Western Schism.

- **Avignon Papacy**: In 1389, the Crown of Aragon recognized Clement VII at Avignon. Royal letters seeking benefices would be directed there.

## 4. HISTORICAL NOTES

### Persons

**Violant de Bar (Queen Violant/Yolande)**: Consort of Joan I of Aragon (r. 1387–1396). French princess, daughter of Robert I, Duke of Bar. Active in Crown finances and diplomacy, particularly regarding her dowry lands and revenues.

**Pere II d'Urgell ("Comte car cosí")**: Count of Urgell (1347–1408). The address "dear cousin" reflects the kinship between the royal house and the Urgell branch of the Crown of Aragon. Important political figure who later contested the succession during the Interregnum.

**Huc de Cervelló (mossèn)**: Noble emissary, likely from the prominent Cervelló lineage of Catalan magnates. The title "mossèn" indicates knightly status.

**Bartolomé Sirvent**: The queen's scribe for the secret seal (*sigillum secretum*), responsible for this entire register series (Curie Sigilli Secreti 1).

### Places

**Monzón (Montço)**: Town in Aragon, site of important Corts/Cortes meetings. The Crown was likely present here in August 1389 for the General Corts of the Crown of Aragon.

### Context: Military Orders and Castilian Negotiations

Document C references negotiations with Castilian ambassadors concerning:
- Properties of the **Order of Calatrava** and **Order of Santiago** 
- Lands held "in pawn" (*penyoria*) by King Joan I
- A sale (*venda*) being negotiated on Queen Violant's behalf

This likely relates to the complex financial arrangements surrounding the queen's dowry, dower properties, and revenues. The military orders held extensive properties in the borderlands between Castile and Aragon, and such transactions often involved both crowns.

## 4. HISTORICAL NOTES

### Persons

**Jean de Valois, Duke of Berry (1340–1416)**
Third son of King John II of France; uncle to Queen Violant de Bar through her mother Marie de France. One of the most powerful French princes during the minority of Charles VI. A renowned patron of the arts (the *Très Riches Heures* was commissioned for him). His correspondence with the Aragonese court reflects the close dynastic ties between the houses of France and Aragon-Barcelona.

**King Joan I of Aragon (r. 1387–1396)**
The letter reports that the king is suffering from "terçana dobla" (double tertian fever), a form of malaria with fever spikes every third day. Joan I was known for poor health throughout his reign.

**Infante Fernando (1389–1416)**
Referred to as "primogenit" (firstborn heir). Born 1389, he died young (1416). This reference confirms the document's 1389 date, as Fernando was born that year.

**Estuier Robinet**
Likely a French messenger or envoy (the name is Occitan/French in form: "Estuier" could be a form of "Esteve" or a title). He appears to have accompanied or delivered the Duke of Berry's letter.

**Bartolomé Sirvent**
Queen Violant's personal secretary, responsible for her secret seal correspondence. His name appears throughout this register.

### Places

**Monzón (Monçó)**
Town in Aragon where the Corts (parliament) of Aragon frequently met. The royal court was evidently residing there in August 1389. Gemini's reading "çoçontijo" is a serious misreading—the manuscript clearly shows the standard form "Monçó."

### Medical Terminology

**Terçana dobla (double tertian fever)**
A severe form of malaria caused by *Plasmodium falciparum*, characterized by fever paroxysms occurring daily rather than every other day (as in simple tertian). This was a common and serious illness in medieval Mediterranean regions.
